title: Magnetism and electromagnetism
blurb: Predict how magnetic poles interact, name ferromagnetic materials, strengthen an electromagnet, and explain motors, generators, transformers and induction.
question: Why must an MRI room be kept free of iron objects, how does a hospital's backup generator make electricity, and why will a transformer not work on a battery?

teach.body: Formally, every magnet has a north pole and a south pole; like poles repel and unlike poles attract. In plain English: north pushes north away and pulls south in. Poles always come in pairs. Cut a bar magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole; you can never isolate a single pole. A compass needle is a small magnet whose north-seeking end points toward Earth's geographic north.

A magnetic field surrounds every magnet. Outside the magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole, and they crowd together where the field is strongest, near the poles. Earth behaves like a giant magnet. Ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt and their alloys, such as steel) are strongly attracted to magnets and can be magnetized. Most other metals, including aluminum, copper and gold, are not.

Moving charges, and so electric currents, produce magnetic fields (Oersted's discovery): a compass needle beside a current-carrying wire swings. Wind the wire into a coil and you get an electromagnet; put an iron core inside and it becomes much stronger. Unlike a permanent magnet, an electromagnet can be switched off. Reversing the current swaps its north and south poles but does not change its strength.

A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force: that is how an electric motor turns electrical energy into mechanical energy. The reverse is electromagnetic induction (Faraday): a CHANGING magnetic field through a coil induces a voltage and current. Move a magnet into a coil and current flows; hold it still and the current stops; pull it out and the current reverses. Generators use induction to turn mechanical energy into electrical energy.

teach.h: Three devices, one set of ideas
teach.caption: A transformer changes AC voltage. Steady DC makes a steady field, which induces nothing, so a transformer does not work on DC.

teach.body: Sam, a radiography applicant, shadows in an MRI suite. The scanner uses a very strong magnetic field plus radio waves, so staff screen out iron, nickel and cobalt objects: ferromagnetic metals are pulled hard toward the magnet, while aluminum is not. In a power cut, the hospital's backup generator spins coils through magnetic fields, and the changing field induces the current that keeps equipment running. Transformers then adjust that AC voltage.

teach.text: Like poles repel. Cutting a magnet never separates north from south. Not all metals are magnetic: aluminum, copper and gold are not. A motor turns electricity into motion; a generator turns motion into electricity. A steady magnetic field, or steady DC, induces no current, which is why transformers need AC. Reversing an electromagnet's current swaps its poles; it does not strengthen it.

items: Like poles repel, unlike attract; every piece of a magnet has both poles.
Field lines run N to S outside the magnet; strongest near the poles.
Electromagnet: stronger with more turns, more current, an iron core; can be switched off.
Motor: electrical to mechanical. Generator: mechanical to electrical by induction. Transformers need AC.

summary: You can now predict how magnetic poles interact, describe magnetic field lines and name the ferromagnetic metals. You can also explain how currents make magnetic fields, how to strengthen an electromagnet, and how motors, generators and transformers use magnetic forces and induction.

A.q: Which pair of magnet ends will attract each other?
A.why: Unlike poles attract: a north pole pulls on a south pole.

whyNot.3: Copper is not ferromagnetic, so a magnet does not noticeably attract it.

A.q: Which of these metals is strongly attracted to a magnet?
A.why: Iron is ferromagnetic, like nickel and cobalt, so it is strongly attracted to magnets.

whyNot.2: Copper is not ferromagnetic; it is used in wires, not magnets.

A.q: Which device converts electrical energy into mechanical energy?
A.why: In a motor, current in a coil within a magnetic field feels a force that turns the shaft: electrical to mechanical.

whyNot.1: A generator does the reverse: mechanical to electrical.
whyNot.2: A transformer changes one AC voltage into another; it produces no motion.
whyNot.3: A compass shows the direction of a magnetic field; it converts no energy for use.

B.q: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?
options: At the middle, between the poles
Far from the magnet, where lines spread
Equally strong at every point around it
Near the poles, where lines crowd
B.why: Field lines are closest together near the poles, which is where the field is strongest.

whyNot.0: The middle of a bar magnet has the weakest pull.
whyNot.1: Spread-out lines show a weaker field.
whyNot.2: The field varies; it is strongest at the poles.

B.q: A compass is placed beside a straight copper wire. When a current is switched on in the wire, what happens?
options: The needle stays put: wires are not magnets
The needle deflects: the current makes a field
The needle spins steadily like a motor
B.why: An electric current produces a magnetic field around the wire, which turns the compass needle (Oersted).

whyNot.0: A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field even though copper is not ferromagnetic.
whyNot.2: A steady current makes a steady field, so the needle turns to a new position and stops.
whyNot.3: The wire's field turns the needle; it does not demagnetize it.

B.q: Which change would NOT make an electromagnet stronger?
options: Adding more turns of wire to it
Adding an iron core inside the coil
B.why: Reversing the current swaps the north and south poles but leaves the strength the same.

whyNot.0: More turns make a stronger electromagnet.
whyNot.1: More current makes a stronger electromagnet.
whyNot.3: An iron core greatly strengthens the field.

C.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a meter, held still inside it, then pulled out. When does current flow in the coil?
options: While it is held still inside
Moving in and out, in opposite directions
Moving in and out, in the same direction
C.why: Current is induced only while the field through the coil is changing. Pushing in and pulling out change it in opposite senses, so the current reverses.

whyNot.0: A still magnet gives a steady field, which induces no current.
whyNot.1: No current flows while the magnet is held still.
whyNot.3: Reversing the motion reverses the induced current.

C.q: Why will a transformer not change the voltage of a car battery?
options: The battery's voltage is too low to flow through coils
Direct current flows backward through the second coil
The battery's steady DC induces no voltage
C.why: A transformer works by induction, which needs a changing magnetic field. A battery's steady DC makes a steady field, so nothing is induced in the second coil.

whyNot.0: Current flows through coils at any voltage; the problem is that it does not change.
whyNot.1: No current is induced in the second coil at all, forward or backward.
whyNot.2: Batteries supply direct current, not alternating current.

C.q: A student cuts a bar magnet in half, then cuts one of the halves in half again. How many north poles are there in total among the pieces?
C.why: There are three pieces, and every piece is a complete magnet with one north and one south pole: 3 north poles.

whyNot.1: Cutting does not leave the original north pole as the only one; each piece gets its own.
whyNot.2: Counts the first cut only; the second cut adds another complete magnet.
whyNot.3: 6 is the total number of poles (north and south), not the north poles alone.

reteach.title: The bike light and the desk fan
reteach.question: A bicycle dynamo lights a lamp when you pedal, and a desk fan spins when you plug it in. How are these the same machine run backward?

blocks.body: Both contain a coil and a magnet. In the dynamo, your pedaling spins the magnet near the coil, the changing field induces a current, and the lamp lights: mechanical in, electrical out, a generator. In the fan, current from the outlet flows through a coil inside a magnetic field, the force on the current turns the blades: electrical in, mechanical out, a motor. Stop pedaling and the field stops changing, so the lamp goes out.

blocks.text: Motion in, electricity out: generator. Electricity in, motion out: motor. Mixing these up is the classic exam slip.

explain.body: A compass needle is a small magnet, so its north end is repelled by another north pole and attracted by a south pole.

test.q: The north end of a bar magnet is brought near the north end of a compass needle. What does the needle's north end do?
test.why: Two north poles repel, so the needle's north end swings away.

whyNot.0: Swinging toward would mean attraction, which happens between unlike poles.
whyNot.2: The magnet's field is strong enough nearby to move the needle.
whyNot.3: A steady magnet turns the needle to a new position; it does not spin it.

explain.body: Steel is mostly iron, so it is ferromagnetic. Aluminum is not, so a magnet does not pick it up.

test.q: A recycling plant uses a large magnet on a conveyor of mixed cans. Which cans does the magnet pull out?
test.why: Steel is an iron alloy, so it is ferromagnetic and attracted to the magnet; aluminum is not.

whyNot.2: Only the iron-based steel cans are ferromagnetic.
whyNot.3: Steel cans are ferromagnetic and are pulled out.

explain.body: An electromagnet's field exists only while current flows, so it can be switched on and off.

test.q: Why do scrapyard cranes use electromagnets rather than permanent magnets?
options: They attract aluminum scrap as well as iron
They can be switched off to drop the load
They are weaker, so they are safer
test.why: Cutting the current switches the field off, so the crane can release the scrap where it wants.

whyNot.0: An electromagnet needs current; that is how it is switched on.
whyNot.1: Aluminum is not ferromagnetic, so electromagnets do not lift it either.
whyNot.3: Crane electromagnets are very strong; their advantage is control, not weakness.

explain.body: Turning a coil in a magnetic field keeps the field through the coil changing, and that change induces a current.

test.q: In a generator, what produces the electric current?
options: A steady magnet beside a still coil
Current fed into the coil from a battery
Friction between the coil and the magnet
A coil turning in a magnetic field
test.why: Turning the coil changes the magnetic field through it, which induces a current (electromagnetic induction).

whyNot.0: A steady field through a still coil induces no current.
whyNot.1: Feeding in current from a battery would run a motor, not a generator.
whyNot.2: Friction produces heat, not the induced current.
